00-hello-world.subject: Teaches the skeleton of every Rust program: an entry point that runs and prints text to the screen.

01-bindings-and-immutability.subject: Teaches that naming a value with let binds it immutably by default so it can't be reassigned later.
teaches: E0384 (cannot assign twice to immutable variable)

02-mutability.subject: Teaches how mut opts a binding into being changeable while keeping its type fixed.
teaches: type stays fixed after first assignment

03-shadowing.subject: Teaches shadowing: a second let with the same name makes a new binding that can change the value's type, unlike mut.
teaches: changing a value's type across bindings

04-constants.subject: Teaches const for values fixed forever and known at compile time, requiring an explicit type.

05-scalar-types.subject: Teaches Rust's four scalar types and that Rust never converts between number types silently.
teaches: integers (i32, u32, u8, i64) and signed/unsigned widths

05b-integer-overflow.subject: Teaches that arithmetic overflowing an integer's width causes a runtime panic in debug builds rather than silent wrapping.
teaches: debug vs release build overflow behavior

06-expressions-statements-semicolon.subject: Teaches the difference between expressions (produce values) and statements, and how a semicolon discards a value to produce unit ().
teaches: blocks as expressions (last line without semicolon)
E0308 from a stray semicolon in a returning function

07-functions.subject: Teaches declaring functions with typed parameters and a return type, returning via the last expression.

08-comments-and-printing.subject: Teaches comment syntax and the full range of printing with println!, format!, and Display vs Debug formatting.

09-if-else.subject: Teaches branching: how to run one block of code when a condition is true and another otherwise, using if/else if/else with real bool conditions (no truthiness).

09b-if-as-expression.subject: Teaches that an if/else is an expression that produces a value, so it can sit on the right of a let, with the requirement that every arm produce the same type.

10-loop-and-break.subject: Teaches the loop keyword that repeats forever until break, and its unique power to carry a value out via break <value> because it has exactly one exit.
teaches: E0571 break with value from a while loop

10b-while.subject: Teaches the while loop that repeats while a bool condition holds, checking the condition each pass and stopping when it becomes false.
teaches: why while cannot break with a value

10c-for-and-ranges.subject: Teaches the for loop that walks each item of a collection or range without managing an index, so it cannot run off the end.
teaches: E0425 cannot find value in this scope

11-match-intro.subject: Teaches match: hand it one value, list cases as patterns, and it runs the first arm that fits, with compiler-enforced exhaustiveness.

12-string-vs-str.subject: Teaches the difference between a borrowed fixed &str view and an owned growable String, and how to build and grow a String.
teaches: E0277 str cannot be indexed by integer

13-tuples.subject: Teaches tuples: bundling a fixed number of values of different types into one value, accessed by destructuring or by position.
teaches: arity as part of the type

13b-arrays.subject: Teaches arrays: a fixed-length row of same-type values whose length is part of the type [T; N], with bounds checks caught at compile time or run time.
teaches: for as the safe fix for indexing

13c-slices.subject: Teaches slices: a borrowed window &[T] into part of a sequence whose type erases the length, so one function accepts any size.
teaches: &str is a slice of a String
runtime panic on out-of-range slice / UTF-8 char-boundary

14-vec.subject: Teaches Vec<T>, the growable list whose length lives at run time, and the deliberate choice between indexing (which panics on a bad index) and .get() (which returns an Option).

14b-hashmap.subject: Teaches HashMap<K,V> as a key-to-value lookup table, including the required import, the entry/or_insert counting idiom, and its unordered nature.

15-ownership.subject: Teaches Rust's ownership model: every value has one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped and freed automatically at build-time-proven safety.
teaches: automatic freeing at end of block

15b-moves.subject: Teaches that assigning or passing a String moves ownership (invalidating the old name) so a value is never freed twice, and using the moved value is Rust's most famous compile error.
teaches: preview of borrowing as the fix

15c-copy-and-clone.subject: Teaches the Copy trait (why small stack values duplicate on assignment instead of moving) versus non-Copy types that move, and .clone() as the explicit, visible deep copy.
teaches: reading the Copy line in E0382

16-shared-references.subject: Teaches shared references (&T) that let code borrow a value to read it without taking ownership, so the original owner keeps the value and can have many simultaneous read-only borrows.
teaches: E0507 (cannot move out of a shared reference)

16b-mutable-references.subject: Teaches mutable references (&mut T) for borrowing to change a value, plus the two borrowing rules (shared xor mutable, references must stay valid) enforced by the borrow checker.

17-slices-in-depth.subject: Teaches that a slice is a borrow pointing into a collection, so while the slice is alive the collection is borrowed immutably — which turns stale-index bugs into compile errors.

18-defining-structs.subject: Teaches defining and instantiating structs to group related fields into one named owned type, including field-init shorthand, struct update, tuple structs, and unit structs.

18b-methods-and-impl.subject: Teaches attaching behaviour to structs via impl blocks and methods, where the receiver (&self / &mut self / self) mirrors the Phase-4 borrow rules, plus associated functions called with ::.

18c-derive-debug.subject: Adding `#[derive(Debug)]` above a struct makes it printable with `{:?}` (compact) and `{:#?}` (pretty), and the compiler literally tells you to add that line when it's missing.

19-enums.subject: An enum models a value that is one of several shapes, with variants that can be empty or carry data, and you attach methods with impl that match on self.

19b-option.subject: Rust has no null; instead the possibility of a missing value lives in the type `Option<T>` (Some/None), so the compiler forces you to handle absence.

19c-match-in-depth.subject: The full match pattern vocabulary — binding inner data, multiple patterns, ranges, guards, and catch-alls — while the compiler still enforces exhaustiveness.

19d-concise-matching.subject: Three short forms — `if let`, `while let`, and `let…else` — handle a single case by deliberately trading away exhaustiveness checking to keep the happy path flat.

20-result.subject: In Rust a recoverable error is an ordinary value carried in the return type as `Result<T, E>` (Ok/Err), which you read with match or unwrap_or rather than hidden exceptions.

20b-panic-unwrap-expect.subject: The blunt error path stops the program on the spot: `panic!` halts the thread, and `unwrap`/`expect` give the Ok/Some value or panic — a runtime crash, not a compile error.

20c-question-mark.subject: The `?` operator is a whole error-handling match in one character: on Err it early-returns the error from the enclosing function, and on Ok it unwraps and continues.
teaches: function must return Result or Option

21-packages-and-crates.subject: Names the units of a Rust project: a crate is the smallest unit the compiler builds (binary with src/main.rs or library with src/lib.rs) and a package is a Cargo.toml plus one or more crates.

21b-modules.subject: A module (`mod`) is a named group inside a crate that provides organization and privacy, and nested modules form a tree rooted at `crate` addressed by `::` paths.

21c-modules-in-files.subject: It teaches how a `mod name;` declaration (semicolon, no body) tells the compiler to load a module's body from a separate file so the directory layout mirrors the module tree.
teaches: "mod is not an include" (declared once, referred to by path)
E0583 file not found for module

22-paths.subject: It teaches how to name an item in another module using `::`-separated paths, distinguishing absolute (crate::) from relative (self::/super::/sibling) forms.
teaches: child modules can call ancestors' private items
E0425 cannot find function in this scope

22b-privacy-and-pub.subject: It teaches that every item is private to code outside its module by default and that `pub` opens one specific item, with the trap that `pub mod` does not make the module's contents public.
teaches: pub mod does not publish contents (two-strike rule)

22c-pub-structs-enums.subject: It teaches the asymmetry that a `pub struct` keeps its fields private (requiring a public constructor) while a `pub enum` makes all its variants public.
teaches: E0616 private field (and E0451 for struct literals)

23-the-use-keyword.subject: It teaches how the `use` keyword brings a path into scope once so code can call items by their short name, plus handling name clashes with `as` and the scope-locality trap.
teaches: as for renaming to avoid clashes
pub use re-exporting and glob/nested imports
E0433 unresolved module in this scope

24-generic-functions.subject: It teaches how a generic type parameter `<T>` lets one function work for many types by leaving a type hole filled at each call, ending copy-paste-and-rename duplication.
teaches: a generic body must be valid for every T
Vec<T> and Option<T> as generics already used
E0369 binary operation > cannot be applied to &T

24b-generic-types.subject: It teaches how to put the `<T>` placeholder into struct definitions, enum definitions, and impl blocks so one type definition serves every element type.
teaches: impl<T> Point<T> with <T> declared after impl
E0425 cannot find type T in this scope

25-traits-declare-implement.subject: It teaches how to declare a trait as a set of method signatures and implement it for a type with `impl Trait for Type`, distinguishing required methods from default methods.
teaches: required (no body) vs default (with body) methods
traits must be in scope to call; the orphan rule
E0046 not all trait items implemented

25b-trait-bounds.subject: It teaches how a trait bound constrains a generic `T` to types implementing a trait so the body may use the trait's behaviour, closing Lesson 24's E0369 wall.

26-lifetime-annotations.subject: It teaches lifetime annotations (`'a`) as generics for how long references stay valid, needed when a function returns one of several input references so the compiler knows which it borrows from.
teaches: fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str
annotations describe relationships, they don't change lifespans
E0597 does not live long enough

26b-lifetime-elision.subject: It explains the compiler's lifetime elision rules — chiefly that a function with one input reference donates that lifetime to all outputs — so you know which functions demand a manual annotation and which don't.
teaches: E0515 (returning a reference to a local)

26c-lifetimes-in-structs.subject: It teaches how to declare a lifetime on a struct so a field can hold a borrowed reference (&'a str) without owning it, guaranteeing the struct never outlives the data it borrows.
teaches: borrow vs own for struct fields

27-closure-syntax.subject: It introduces closures as anonymous inline functions written with |param| bars, saved in variables or passed to methods, whose parameter/return types are inferred and locked on first use.
teaches: type inference locked on first use
passing closures to methods like sort_by_key

27b-closure-capture.subject: It teaches how closures capture surrounding variables in one of three ways (immutable borrow, mutable borrow, or take ownership), with the body deciding the mode and the move keyword forcing ownership.
teaches: E0507 (cannot move out of captured variable)

28-iterator-cursor.subject: It reveals that a for loop is driven by an iterator — a cursor implementing the Iterator trait whose next() returns Some/None — and that iter/iter_mut/into_iter choose read, mutate, or take-ownership access.

28b-adapter-chains.subject: It teaches building readable iterator pipelines from lazy adapters (map, filter) plus a consumer (collect, sum) that actually drives the work, and why a chain with no consumer does nothing.
teaches: collect consumer and its type annotation

29-box.subject: It introduces Box<T> as a smart pointer that stores a value on the heap behind a fixed-size pointer, chiefly to give recursive self-containing types a known size via indirection.

29b-deref-drop.subject: It explains the two traits behind smart pointers: Deref (why * follows a box like a reference) and Drop (an automatic cleanup hook that runs at scope-end in reverse creation order).

29c-rc.subject: It teaches Rc<T> as a reference-counted smart pointer enabling multiple shared read-only owners of one heap value, cleaned up only when the count reaches zero.
teaches: Rc::clone (cheap count bump, not data copy)

29d-refcell.subject: It teaches RefCell<T> as interior mutability — mutating a value through a shared, immutable-looking handle by moving the borrow check to runtime, panicking on violation, and combining with Rc as Rc<RefCell<T>>.
teaches: runtime borrow checking (panic vs compile error)

30-spawning-threads.subject: How to start a second line of work with a thread and safely hand it data, using thread::spawn to run a closure, join to wait for it, and move to give the thread ownership so borrows can't dangle.

30b-channels.subject: How threads cooperate without sharing by sending values through a one-way channel, where send moves ownership so the sender can no longer touch the value.

30c-shared-state.subject: How multiple threads safely share and mutate one value using Arc for many owners and Mutex for exclusive access, with the compiler's errors steering you to the Arc<Mutex<T>> design.

31-async-syntax.subject: The shape of async code: async fn returns a future rather than its value, async blocks are future-valued expressions, and .await runs a future to completion inside async contexts.
teaches: async vs threads (cooperative concurrency vs parallelism)

31b-futures-are-lazy.subject: The core async rule that a future does nothing until driven, which is why async code needs a runtime and why .await is restricted and main cannot be async on its own.
teaches: async fn main is not allowed

32-trait-objects.subject: How dyn Trait behind a pointer lets one collection or function hold many different concrete types and call their shared method via runtime dynamic dispatch.

32b-encapsulation.subject: How keeping struct fields private and exposing only public methods enforces invariants in one place and lets you change internals without breaking callers.

32c-states-as-types.subject: How giving each stage its own type (e.g. DraftPost vs PublishedPost) makes wrong-state operations unrepresentable, with transitions that consume self to retire the old state.

33-refutability.subject: The refutability rule that governs where patterns may sit: irrefutable patterns (always match) are needed for let/for/params, while refutable ones (can fail) require an else path via if let/while let/match.
teaches: if let / let...else provide the else path
irrefutable if let is only a warning

33b-guards-bindings-nested.subject: Three pattern power tools for match: match guards add a value condition to an arm, @ bindings capture a value while range-testing it, and nested destructuring reaches into layered data.
teaches: match guards (if condition on an arm)

34-unsafe.subject: It teaches that `unsafe` is a small, auditable block that unlocks five compiler-unverifiable abilities (chiefly dereferencing raw pointers) without disabling the borrow checker.
teaches: unsafe blocks and the five superpowers
raw pointers *const T / *mut T and &raw const / &raw mut
dereferencing a raw pointer requires unsafe (E0133)
unsafe does not turn off borrow checking (E0502)

34b-operator-overloading.subject: It teaches operator overloading by implementing std::ops traits like Add on your own type, and explains associated types (type Output) so you can read forms like Future<Output = u32>.
teaches: a + b is sugar for Add::add(a, b)
associated types via type Output and type Item
E0369 cannot add before implementing Add

34c-macro-rules.subject: It teaches declarative macros with macro_rules! — pattern-to-template rules that generate code before compilation — by building a stripped-down my_vec! macro.
teaches: macros expand before compilation, marked by !

35-single-threaded-server.subject: It builds a real single-threaded HTTP server with TcpListener/TcpStream so the learner feels why handling connections inline (one at a time) stalls behind a slow request.
teaches: anatomy of an HTTP response (status line, headers, blank line, body)
E0596 missing mut on the stream parameter

35b-thread-pool.subject: It fixes the single-threaded server by building a fixed-size thread pool with workers pulling boxed closure jobs from a shared channel, plus graceful shutdown via Drop and join.
teaches: ThreadPool with workers and an mpsc channel
graceful shutdown with Drop, Option::take, and join
worker lock-scope releasing the guard before running a job

36-automated-tests.subject: It teaches writing automated tests that pass when they don't panic, using #[test] functions, assertion macros, and #[should_panic], run by cargo test.
teaches: assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne! (a test passes if it doesn't panic)
reading a failing test's left/right output

37-doc-comments.subject: It teaches Markdown doc comments (/// and //!) that cargo doc renders into an HTML manual, and doc-tests — code examples that cargo test compiles and runs so docs can't drift from code.
teaches: /// documents the item below; //! documents the enclosing item
Markdown doc comments and cargo doc --open
doc-tests: fenced examples run by cargo test
# Examples sections as part of the test suite
a lying doc example fails with left/right mismatch

37b-shipping-with-cargo.subject: It surveys Cargo's shipping toolkit: release vs dev build profiles, publishing crates to crates.io with required metadata, workspaces of related crates, and cargo install.
teaches: cargo publish with required [package] description and license (yank is permanent, no delete)
workspaces ([workspace] members, shared Cargo.lock and target/)
measuring speed with --release, not the dev build
